title: VI. The Prosecutor’s Speech. Sketches Of Character
paragraphs: Ippolit Kirillovitch began his speech trembling with nerves, cold sweat on his forehead, flashing hot and cold by turns. He said so himself afterward. He considered this speech his masterpiece — the masterpiece of his whole life, his swan song. And in fact he died nine months later of galloping consumption, so it turned out he'd had the right to compare himself to a swan singing its last song. He had put his whole heart and every ounce of brain he had into that speech. And to everyone's surprise, poor Ippolit Kirillovitch turned out to have at least some genuine feeling for the public good and for “the eternal question” hidden away in him. What really set his speech apart was its sincerity. He truly believed the prisoner was guilty; he wasn't prosecuting merely as an official duty, and when he called for retribution he trembled with real passion “for the safety of society.” Even the women in the audience, who stayed hostile to Ippolit Kirillovitch throughout, admitted he made an extraordinary impression on them. He began in a cracking voice, but it gained strength as he went and filled the courtroom by the end of his speech. Yet the moment he finished, he nearly fainted.

“Gentlemen of the jury,” the prosecutor began, “this case has caused a stir across all of Russia. But what is there to be amazed at, really — what is so uniquely horrifying about it to us? That's what's so horrifying: that we've grown so used to crimes like this. What ought to appall us is not this or that isolated crime, but the fact that we've become accustomed to it. What accounts for our indifference, our lukewarm response to acts like this, to these signs of the times, ominous as they are for an unpromising future? Is it cynicism? Is it a premature exhaustion of intellect and imagination in a society sinking into decay despite its youth? Is it that our moral principles have been shaken to their foundations, or perhaps that we have no such principles at all? I can't answer these questions, and yet they trouble me, and every citizen not only must but ought to be troubled by them. Our young and still timid press has already done the public a real service, because without it we would never have learned of the horrors of unchecked violence and moral collapse that the papers keep bringing to light — not just to those who attend the new jury courts set up under the present reign, but to everyone. And what do we read almost every day? Things next to which this case pales, seems almost ordinary. But the important point is that most of our national crimes of violence testify to a widespread evil, now so general among us that it's hard to fight.”

“One day we see a brilliant young officer from high society, at the very start of his career, coldly and treacherously, without a flicker of conscience, murdering an official who had once been his benefactor, along with the man's servant girl, in order to steal his own promissory note and whatever cash he could find on him — ‘it'll come in handy for my pleasures in fashionable society, and for my career.’ After killing them, he tucks a pillow under each victim's head, then leaves. Next, a young war hero ‘decorated for bravery’ kills the mother of his commanding officer and benefactor, like a common highwayman, and to talk his accomplices into it he insists that ‘she loves him like a son, so she'll follow all his instructions and take no precautions.’ Granted, he's a monster — but I don't dare claim these days that he's unique. Another man won't commit the murder, but will feel and think exactly as he does, and is every bit as rotten in his soul. Alone, in silence, with only his conscience for company, he may ask himself, ‘What is honor, really — and isn't condemning bloodshed just a prejudice?’”

“Perhaps people will accuse me of being morbid, hysterical, of monstrous slander, of exaggeration. Let them say so — and heaven knows, I'd be the first to rejoice if it were true! Oh, don't believe me — think of me as sick in the head if you like, but remember my words: even if only a tenth, only a twentieth, of what I say is true, it's still appalling! Look how our young people kill themselves, without so much as asking Hamlet's question about what lies beyond, without any sign that such a question has crossed their minds — as though everything to do with the soul, with what awaits us past the grave, had long ago been erased from their heads and buried in the sand. Look at our vice, our libertines. Fyodor Pavlovitch, the unlucky victim in this case, was practically an innocent babe next to many of them. And yet we all knew him — ‘he lived among us!’...”

“Yes — perhaps someday the great minds of Russia and of Europe will study the psychology of Russian crime, because the subject deserves it. But that study will come later, at leisure, once all of today's tragic upheaval lies further behind us, when it can be examined with more insight and more fairness than I can manage now. For the moment we're either horrified, or pretend to be, while actually gloating over the spectacle, drawn to strong and eccentric sensations that titillate our cynical, pampered boredom. Or else, like children, we brush the terrible ghosts away and bury our heads in the pillow, eager to get back to our games and amusements the moment they're gone. But someday we'll have to start living in sober earnest; we'll have to look at ourselves as a society; it's time we tried to understand something of our own social condition, or at least made a start in that direction.”

“A great writer of the last generation, comparing Russia to a swift troika racing toward an unknown destination, cries out, ‘Oh, troika, bird-like troika, who invented you!’ and adds, in proud ecstasy, that all the nations of the world stand respectfully aside to let the recklessly galloping troika pass. Maybe so — maybe they do stand aside, respectfully or not — but in my humble opinion the great writer ended his book that way either in a fit of childish, naïve optimism, or simply out of fear of the censors of his day. Because if the troika were being driven by his own heroes — Sobakevitch, Nozdryov, Tchitchikov — it could never reach any rational destination, no matter who held the reins. And those were the heroes of an older generation. Ours are worse specimens still....”

At this point Ippolit Kirillovitch's speech was interrupted by applause. The liberal implications of the image were not lost on anyone. The applause was brief, true, so the presiding judge didn't think it necessary to issue a warning, and only gave the offenders a stern look. But Ippolit Kirillovitch was encouraged — he had never been applauded before! All his life he had struggled to get anyone to listen to him, and now, suddenly, he had a chance to command the ear of all Russia.

“What, in the end, is this Karamazov family, which has earned such an unenviable notoriety across Russia?” he went on. “Perhaps I'm exaggerating, but it seems to me that certain fundamental traits of today's educated class are reflected in this family portrait — only, of course, in miniature, ‘like the sun in a drop of water.’ Think of that unhappy, depraved, unrestrained old man who met such a grim end — the head of a family! Born into the nobility, but in a poor, dependent position, he came into a small fortune through an unexpected marriage. A petty schemer, a toady and a buffoon, with a fairly sharp though undeveloped mind, he was above all a moneylender, growing bolder as his fortunes grew. His fawning, servile side dropped away, leaving only his malicious, sarcastic cynicism. Spiritually he never developed at all, while his appetite for life was excessive. He saw nothing in life but sensual pleasure, and he raised his children to see nothing else either. He felt no obligation to his duties as a father — he mocked them. He left his young children to the servants and was glad to be rid of them, forgot about them entirely. The old man's motto was Après moi le déluge. He stood for everything opposed to civic duty, the most complete and vicious individualism. ‘Let the world burn, so long as I'm all right’ — and he was all right; he was content, eager to keep living exactly this way for another twenty or thirty years. He cheated his own son, spending the boy's money — his inheritance from his mother — trying to steal his mistress from him. No, I don't intend to leave the prisoner's defense entirely to my talented colleague from Petersburg. I'll speak the truth myself: I understand perfectly well what resentment must have built up in the son's heart against him.”

“But enough, enough about that unhappy old man — he's paid the price. Let's remember, though, that he was a father, and one of the typical fathers of our time. Am I really being unfair in calling him typical of a great many modern fathers? Alas — plenty of them differ from him only in not openly flaunting such cynicism, because they're better educated, more cultured, but their underlying philosophy is essentially the same as his. Perhaps I'm a pessimist — but you've agreed to forgive me that. Let's agree in advance: you don't have to believe me, but let me speak. Let me say what I have to say, and hold on to a little of it.”
“Now, the children of this father, this head of a family. One of them is the prisoner before us — the rest of my speech will deal with him. Of the other two I'll speak only in passing.”

“The eldest son is one of those modern young men of brilliant education and vigorous intellect who has lost all faith in everything. He has already denied and rejected a great deal, like his father. We've all heard him speak; he was a welcome guest in local society. He never hid his views — quite the opposite, in fact — which is my justification for speaking rather openly about him now, not as an individual, of course, but as a member of the Karamazov family. Another figure closely tied to this case took his own life here just last night. I mean the afflicted, feeble-minded man who had been Fyodor Pavlovitch's servant, and possibly his illegitimate son — Smerdyakov. At the preliminary inquiry he told me, in tears, hysterically, how young Ivan Karamazov had appalled him with his spiritual daring. ‘Everything in the world is permitted, according to him, and nothing will be forbidden from now on — that's what he always taught me.’ I believe that poor, feeble-minded man was driven out of his senses by this theory, though of course the epileptic fits he suffered from, and this terrible catastrophe, no doubt helped unhinge his mind further. But he let drop one remark, quite striking, that would have done credit to a more intelligent observer, and that's exactly why I mention it: ‘If there's one of the sons who takes after Fyodor Pavlovitch in character, it's Ivan Fyodorovitch.’”

“With that remark I'll close my sketch of his character — I feel it would be indelicate to go further. Oh, I have no wish to draw further conclusions and croak over the young man's future like some raven of doom. We've seen today, in this courtroom, that there are still good impulses in his young heart, that family feeling has not been destroyed in him by his lack of faith and his cynicism — traits that came to him more by inheritance, I think, than through any exercise of his own independent thought.”

“Then the third son. Oh, he's a devout, modest young man, who doesn't share his elder brother's bleak, destructive view of life. He has tried to hold fast to ‘the ideas of the people,’ or to whatever goes by that name in certain circles of our educated class. He clung to the monastery, and came within a hair of becoming a monk. It seems to me he unconsciously betrayed, and at such an early age, that timid despair which drives so many in our unhappy society — people who dread cynicism and its corrupting influence, and mistakenly blame all our troubles on European enlightenment — to return to their ‘native soil,’ as they call it, to the bosom, so to speak, of their mother earth, like frightened children longing to fall asleep against the withered breast of their aged mother, and to sleep there forever, if only to escape the horrors that terrify them.”

“For my part, I wish the excellent, gifted young man every success. I hope his youthful idealism and his pull toward the ideas of the people never degenerate, as so often happens, into gloomy mysticism on the spiritual side and blind chauvinism on the political — two forces that pose an even greater danger to Russia than the premature decay, born of misunderstanding and the wholesale borrowing of European ideas, from which his elder brother is suffering.”

Two or three people clapped at the mention of chauvinism and mysticism. Ippolit Kirillovitch had, in truth, been swept away by his own eloquence. None of this had much to do with the case at hand — not to mention that it was rather vague — but the sickly, consumptive man was overcome by the urge to express himself, just once, in his life. People said afterward that his criticism of Ivan was driven by less than noble motives, since Ivan had gotten the better of him once or twice in argument, and Ippolit Kirillovitch, remembering it, was now taking his revenge. But I don't know whether that's true. In any case, all this was only introductory, and the speech now moved on to a more direct look at the case.

“But to return to the eldest son,” Ippolit Kirillovitch went on. “He is the prisoner before us. We have his life, and his actions too, laid out before us; the fatal day has come, and everything has risen to the surface. While his brothers seem to stand for ‘Europeanism’ and ‘the principles of the people,’ he seems to represent Russia as she actually is. Oh, not all of Russia — not all of her! God forbid it should be so! And yet here she is, our mother Russia, her very scent and sound. Oh, he is spontaneous — a marvelous jumble of good and evil, a lover of culture and of Schiller, and yet he brawls in taverns and yanks the beards of his drinking companions. Oh, he too can be good, even noble — but only when things are going well for him. What's more, he can be swept off his feet, positively carried away, by noble ideals — but only if they come to him unbidden, if they drop from heaven, if he doesn't have to pay for them. He hates paying for anything, but he loves receiving, and that's true of him in everything. Oh, give him every good thing life has to offer — he wouldn't be satisfied with less — put no obstacle in his way, and he'll show you that he too can be noble. He isn't greedy — no — but he has to have money, a great deal of money, and you'll see how generously, with what contempt for filthy lucre, he'll fling it all away in one night of reckless dissipation. But if he has no money, you'll see what he's prepared to do to get it when he needs it badly enough. But all that comes later — let's take events in their order.”

“First we have before us a poor, neglected child, running around the back yard ‘without boots on his feet,’ as our worthy and esteemed fellow citizen of foreign extraction — alas! — put it just now. I say again, I yield the defense of the accused to no one. I am here to accuse him, but to defend him too. Yes, I too am human; I too can weigh the influence of home and childhood on a man's character. But the boy grows up and becomes an officer; for a duel, and other reckless behavior, he's exiled to one of Russia's remote frontier towns. There he led the wild life of an officer. And of course he needed money — money above everything — and so, after long disputes, he came to a settlement with his father, and the last six thousand roubles were sent to him. There's a letter in existence in which he essentially waives his claim to the rest and settles his dispute with his father over the inheritance for that payment of six thousand.”

“Then came his meeting with a young woman of lofty character and brilliant education. Oh, I won't presume to repeat the details — you've only just heard them. Honor, self-sacrifice, were on display there, and I'll say no more. The figure of the young officer, frivolous and dissolute, paying homage to true nobility and a lofty ideal, appeared before us in a very sympathetic light. But the other side of the coin was unexpectedly turned toward us immediately afterward, in this very courtroom. Again I won't venture to guess why it happened that way, but there were reasons. That same lady, her eyes wet with tears of long-suppressed indignation, told us that he — he, of all men — had despised her for an act which, reckless and imprudent as it may have been, was still prompted by lofty and generous motives. He, the girl's own betrothed, looked at her with that mocking smile, more unbearable coming from him than from anyone else. And knowing already that he had deceived her — believing, as he did, that she was bound to endure anything from him, even betrayal — she deliberately offered him three thousand roubles, and let him understand, all too clearly, that she was paying him to deceive her. ‘Well — will you take it or not? Have you no shame at all?’ was the silent question in her searching eyes. He looked at her, saw plainly what was in her mind — he's admitted before you here that he understood all of it — and pocketed those three thousand roubles without a second thought, then squandered them in two days on his new love.”

“What are we to believe, then? The first version — of the young officer sacrificing his last farthing in a noble burst of generosity, doing homage to virtue — or this other, repellent picture? As a rule, when faced with two extremes, one looks for the middle ground — but in this case that won't do. It's more likely that in the first instance he was genuinely noble, and in the second, genuinely base. And why? Because he has the broad Karamazov nature — that's exactly what I'm building toward — capable of combining the most incongruous contradictions, capable of the greatest heights and the greatest depths at once. Remember the brilliant observation made by a young man who has watched the Karamazov family up close — Mr. Rakitin: ‘The sense of their own degradation is as essential to these reckless, ungoverned natures as the sense of their own lofty generosity.’ And that's true — they need this unnatural mixture continually. Two extremes at the same moment, or else they feel wretched, dissatisfied, incomplete. They are as broad as mother Russia herself; they take in everything and endure everything.”

“By the way, gentlemen of the jury, since we've just touched on those three thousand roubles, I'll venture to get a little ahead of myself. Can you really imagine a man like that — having received that sum, and in such a way, at the cost of such shame, such disgrace, such utter degradation — could have been capable, that very same day, of setting aside half the sum, sewing it into a little bag, and having the strength of character to carry it on him for a whole month afterward, in spite of every temptation and his desperate need for it! Not once, whether in drunken debauchery in taverns, or when he was racing out into the countryside trying to borrow, from God knows whom, the money he so badly needed to keep the woman he loved out of his father's clutches, did he bring himself to touch that little bag! Why, if only to keep from abandoning his mistress to the rival he was so jealous of, he'd surely have opened that bag and stayed behind to watch over her, waiting for the moment she would finally say to him, ‘I am yours,’ so that he could fly off with her, far from those fatal surroundings.”

“But no — he never touched his talisman, and what reason does he give for that? The main reason, as I've just said, was that when she said ‘I am yours, take me wherever you like,’ he wanted to have the means to take her. But that first reason, in the prisoner's own words, mattered little next to the second. As long as I have that money on me, he said, I am a scoundrel, but not a thief — because I can always go to my insulted betrothed and, laying down half the sum I fraudulently took, say to her, ‘You see, I've squandered half your money, and shown myself weak and dishonorable, a scoundrel if you like’ (I'm using the prisoner's own words) ‘— but though I'm a scoundrel, I'm not a thief, because if I were a thief, I wouldn't have brought you back this half — I'd have taken it too, the way I took the rest!’ A remarkable explanation! This frantic but weak man, who couldn't resist the temptation of taking three thousand roubles at the price of such disgrace, suddenly develops the most stoical willpower and carries around a thousand roubles without daring to touch it. Does that square at all with the character we've just examined? No — and I'll go so far as to tell you how the real Dmitri Karamazov would have behaved in such circumstances, if he had actually brought himself to set the money aside.”

“At the very first temptation — say, to treat the woman with whom he'd already squandered half the money — he would have unpicked the little bag and pulled out a hundred roubles or so. Because why, exactly, would he have kept back precisely half the money — fifteen hundred roubles? Why not fourteen hundred? He could just as easily have claimed he wasn't a thief by bringing back fourteen hundred. Then, another time, he'd have unpicked it again and taken out another hundred, and then a third time, and a fourth, and before the month was out he'd have taken the second-to-last note, reasoning that bringing back even a hundred would serve the purpose, since a thief would have stolen the whole lot. And then he'd have looked at that last note and told himself, ‘It's really not worth handing back just a hundred — let's spend that too!’ That's how the real Dmitri Karamazov, as we know him, would have behaved. Nothing could be harder to reconcile with the actual facts than this legend of the little bag. Nothing could be less conceivable. But we'll return to that later.”

After touching on what had come out at the trial concerning the financial dealings between father and son, and arguing again and again that it was utterly impossible, from the known facts, to say which of them was in the wrong, Ippolit Kirillovitch moved on to the medical experts' testimony regarding Mitya's fixed idea about the three thousand roubles owed him.
